title: Business Logic Errors
description: Handle domain-specific errors like conflicts, constraint violations, and state transitions with precise HTTP status codes and actionable error messages.

data.text: Business logic errors occur when a request is syntactically valid but violates a domain rule. Examples include booking an already-sold seat, transferring money with insufficient balance, or canceling an order that has already shipped. These errors need specific status codes and clear explanations.

data.title: 409 Conflict when booking an already-sold seat
data.content: The error tells the client which resource is conflicted and what the current state is.

data.text: Many business errors are invalid state transitions. Model your entities as state machines and return the current state and allowed transitions in the error response.

items: Define valid states explicitly in your domain model
Return 422 when a transition is not allowed from the current state
Include the current state and allowed next states in the error body
Use a generic 'InvalidStateTransition' code and document the mapping

data.title: 422 when attempting an invalid state transition
data.content: Order transitions: PENDING -> CONFIRMED -> SHIPPED -> DELIVERED. Cannot cancel after SHIPPED.
data.code:
POST /orders/ord_991/cancel

Response: 422 Unprocessable Entity
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/invalid-state-transition",

data.title: 409 is for resource conflicts, not validation
data.text: 409 Conflict means the resource state prevents the operation. Use it for duplicates and locks. Use 422 for semantic errors like insufficient funds where the request is valid but the business rule fails.

items.question: Should I return the current resource state in 409 errors?
items.answer: Yes. Include the current state in the resource object. This lets the client refresh and show the updated state without an extra GET request.

items.question: How do I handle idempotent retries for business errors?
items.answer: Use idempotency keys for all write operations. If the same request is retried, return the same result. For 409 errors, the second retry should still fail with 409.

items.question: Should I distinguish between 'already exists' and 'conflict with another user'?
items.answer: Yes. Use separate error codes: DuplicateEmail for uniqueness violations, ResourceLocked for concurrent modification by another user. Clients handle these differently.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Business errors need specific codes, not generic messages.
Include the current state and allowed transitions in state-machine errors.
Use 409 for conflicts, 422 for semantic violations.
Idempotency keys make retries safe even for business errors.
data.takeaway: Business logic errors are where your API's domain expertise shows. Make them specific, actionable, and safe to retry.
